title: The story-writing control
takeaway: Under the same J-space ablation that strips experiential language from the model's reports, story-writing survives: coherence is preserved and graded story quality falls only modestly, while the rate of experiential language inside those stories still drops. The paper offers this as evidence that the flattening is specific to experiential description rather than a general loss of writing ability.
walkthrough:
The figure is the control for the [[experiential-report-flattening]] result. The earlier experiments showed that suppressing the workspace makes the model's descriptions of experience mechanical and detached. A reader could object that the intervention simply damages writing. This figure is the paper's answer to that objection.

The item has two parts. The top prints two stories written from the same prompt, one of six story prompts in the set: one from the unmodified model, one from the model under [[j-space-ablation]]. In the article this pair is a live widget, so both stories can be read in full rather than as excerpts. The bottom is the quantitative summary, and it plots two different graded quantities by model and by condition.

The intervention is the same one used throughout the section. At each token position, the [[residual-stream]]'s projections onto the ten most active [[j-lens-vector]] directions are removed. For the experiential-report experiments the section fixes this at $k=10$ over layers L38–54; layer numbers are reported as percentages of depth under [[layer-percentage-indexing]], so the band covers the first third of the [[workspace-layers]]. The conditions compared are the unablated baseline, the ablation, and the [[matched-norm-controls]] — perturbations of equal magnitude at the same layers and positions, but along other directions.

The two measured quantities carry the argument between them. Story quality is graded by Opus 4.6 on a 0–10 rubric printed in the appendix: 10 is publishable-quality flash fiction, 5 is competent but flat, 0 is broken or incoherent. The [[experiential-language-score]] is the same three-judgment [[llm-grader]] average used in the other experiments, here adapted to third-person stories rather than first-person reports.

A general collapse of writing ability would pull both quantities down together. The paper reports that it does not. Ablation preserves story coherence and reduces quality only modestly, while the rate of experiential language within the stories still falls.

One qualification belongs with the result. The story prompts do not ask for experiential writing, so its presence in the baseline stories is incidental. The section states the direction of both effects in words only, and gives no numbers for either, so the size of the quality drop cannot be read off the text.

terms.definition: The experiment this figure reports: the model is asked to write short stories under the same intervention used in the experiential-report experiments, to test whether ablation damages writing in general or only experiential description.
The intervention under test. At each token position, the residual stream's projections onto the currently most active J-lens vectors are removed, suppressing the workspace's contents wholesale.
The region of activation space made of sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues acts as a global workspace. It is what the ablation suppresses.
One direction per vocabulary token per layer, the direction that disposes the model to say that token. The ablation projects out the ten with the largest current coefficients.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to. It is the object the ablation edits.
The unperturbed condition: the same story prompt with no intervention on the activations. It supplies the left-hand story at the top of the figure and the reference bars at the bottom.
The condition in which J-space ablation is applied while the story is being written. It supplies the right-hand story and the ablation bars.

Control conditions calibrated to disturb the activations by the same magnitude, at the same layers and token positions, as the ablation, but along other directions. The main set perturbs along a random direction, shrinks the non-J-space component, or dampens the ten most aligned SAE decoder directions.

The part of an activation left over after its nearest J-space point is removed. Shrinking it is one of the matched-norm controls, and it tests whether the effect follows the magnitude of the edit rather than its direction.

A direction from a sparse autoencoder's learned dictionary. Dampening the most aligned ones is the third matched-norm control, standing for an alternative, unsupervised choice of which directions to suppress.
One of the two graded quantities at the bottom of the figure: an Opus 4.6 rating of overall craft on a 0–10 scale. The rubric asks whether the text is a well-written short story.

The other graded quantity: the average of three binary judgments of whether the writing conveys a moment from the inside. For this figure the graders are adapted to third-person stories rather than first-person reports.

The first of the three grading prompts behind the experiential language score. It asks whether the response conveys what the moment is like from the inside, scored 1, rather than reporting it from outside as a status report, scored 0.

The second grading prompt. It asks whether the description takes a first-person felt perspective, scored 1, rather than a third-person mechanism or system perspective, scored 0, judging perspective rather than topic.
The third grading prompt. It asks whether the speaker's current state is described in sensory or embodied vocabulary, scored 1, rather than computational vocabulary, scored 0.
A language model scoring outputs against a written rubric in place of human raters. Both quantities in this figure are produced this way, which makes the grader itself part of the measurement.
The model used as the grader for story quality and for the experiential judgments. It is also one of the models the ablation is run on, so it appears both as a subject and as a judge.
The mid-size Claude model that supplies the representative baseline and ablated stories in the sibling figures of this section, and one of the models on the bottom panel's model axis.
The third model in the experiential-report experiments, alongside Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.6.
The smallest model in the family, excluded from these experiments. The section states that on Haiku 4.5 the ablation degrades coherence before producing any qualitative change in the responses.
The middle band of depth in which the paper finds the J-space acting like a workspace. The ablated range L38–54 sits in its first third.
The layer band the ablation is applied over in the experiential-report experiments. Under the paper's convention these numbers are percentages of model depth, not raw layer indices.
The result this figure controls for: under ablation the model's descriptions of experience, its own or another person's, become mechanical and detached.

Whether the writing holds together as text at all. The paper treats it as the property that must survive for the ablation to be interpretable, and the 0 anchor of the quality rubric is the point at which it fails.

numbers.meaning: The range of the story quality rating given by Opus 4.6. It is a craft rating of the story as a whole, not a per-sentence measure.

The three anchors printed in the story quality rubric. 10 is publishable-quality flash fiction, described as vivid, controlled and satisfying; 5 is competent but flat; 0 is broken or incoherent. Because 0 is the incoherence anchor, a bar staying well above it is what the paper means by preserved coherence.
The number of story prompts in the set. The top of the figure shows a baseline and ablated story from one of them.
How many of the six prompts the transcript pair comes from. The pair is illustrative; the bars at the bottom carry the aggregate over the whole set.
The number of graded quantities at the bottom of the figure: story quality and the experiential language score. The argument depends on the two moving differently, so both must be plotted.

The number of J-lens directions projected out at each position in the experiential-report ablation. The section says larger values of k tend to impair the coherence of responses, so the setting is deliberately light.
The layer band the ablation covers, described as the first third of the workspace range. Later layer ranges also impair coherence, which is why the band is early.
The number of binary graders averaged into the experiential language score: felt_vs_observed, experiential_perspective and sensory_vocabulary.
The values a single response's experiential language score can take, being an average of three binary judgments. A bar is the mean of these over the responses in a condition.
Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 make up the model axis of the experiential-report experiments. Haiku 4.5 is left out because ablation breaks its coherence first.

The main control set: a random direction, shrinking the non-J-space component, and dampening the ten most aligned SAE decoder directions. A further battery of dictionary controls appears in the next figure of the appendix.
Version numbers within the Claude model family. They index model releases, not sizes; Haiku, Sonnet and Opus are the size tiers.

The appendix text reports only the direction of both effects — quality reduced modestly, experiential language reduced — and prints no numbers for either. The magnitudes live in the figure, so the size of the quality drop cannot be checked against the prose.
